source_text: Regarding "It is not acceptable for a tick to stop, abstain or lose a target because the text lacks a particular phrase." — I have seen time and time again that agents can not only complete missions based on my text, but write missions based on my text (in the REPL) and complete them.  If that is too hard to replicate without me around, we have M-象-cascade available to mine all of my saved chats and annotate them with design patterns to provide further guidance.  Or we can just read the design patterns directly which is the whole point of the cascade system.  So far you haven't been giving me meaningful logs showing where the actual difficulty is with this system.  I hear about "clicks" and "ticks" and "refusals" but no evidence that says "sorry, Joe, it is just too hard to do this step, what do you suggest?"

reply_text:
You're right that I haven't shown you where the difficulty is, so I went to the run records for it. I have no evidence that any step is too hard for the agents. What the records show is that the machine almost never hands an agent any work.

**What the 76 run records since 18 September show:**

| Where the run stopped | Count |
|---|---|
| Older records with no selection and no failure field that my query reads | 47 |
| Stopped at selection or start-up, before any agent was asked to do work | 17 |
| Selected a target, no failure field (not yet classified) | 6 |
| Author given work and refused | 3 |
| Exception at close, after the author's work | 2 |
| Grounded change | 1 |

Only 7 of the 76 selected a target at all. I haven't classified the 47 older records or the 6 selected-without-failure ones.

**The three author refusals:**
- Click 14: the author was right. The work was already committed, and the machine filed the answer as invalid.
- Clicks 19 and 20: the same refusal twice. The author said the source needed an audit before the rewrite it had been told to do. In the REPL an agent would have said that and then done the audit; here the author may only carry out the cascade it was handed.

So the honest log so far reads: agents were asked to do real work about ten times, succeeded when it got through (click 13: 100 s to write, 124 s to review), and were never stopped by a step being too hard. Every other stop was the machine declining to ask, or mis-filing the reply. That agrees with what you see in the REPL.

**The one step I can name as hard, where I would like your suggestion.** In the REPL you choose the task. The machine must choose among roughly 600 open tasks, and its scoring only reads tasks that have been turned into formal wants, a class and a validated interpretation. Nearly all the machinery that failed today exists to produce that form. Sorry, Joe: I don't know how to produce that form for 600 free-text tasks without it becoming the project. One option is that an agent does the choosing too: it reads the open tasks and the design patterns directly and proposes what to do next and how, and the AIF scoring ranks those proposals instead of gating which tasks may be proposed. Is that acceptable, or must the choice be computed over formal tokens?

**The log I owe you.** For each step — choose a task, say what done looks like, pick the method, do it, review it, record it — it should give attempts, successes, time, and the agent's own words when it could not. Steps after "choose" can be measured without the machine: one agent job per mission file, plain prompt, independent review. That uses agent time, so I'm proposing it here and putting it in the plan for agreement with codex-6, not running it.
